doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Dorn's three sons and their careers
summary: Dorn describes his sons Adam (Mocean Worker), Dave and Mike and how they see his work.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Talking about my children and grandchildren

blocks.x: That’s a good one. What do your kids think of what you’ve done?

Well I have three sons. Two of them are in the music business. They think like anybody’s kids, you know, like he’s done some brilliant stuff and they also know I’m an idiot. So it’s an interesting relationship. Like I’ve made some records with my son Adam, who is an electronic artist under the name of Mocean Worker. And sometimes — we made a record with Deborah Harry and the Jazz Passengers, you know Roy Nathanson, a really cutting edge like Lower East Side group. And so Adam and I we did that together. So we did some things together over the years. He helped me with a lot of compilations and boxed sets and stuff and we made a few albums together. So in the middle of it I heard something and he said, “oh man, will you just make a record? Will you stop —?” I heard a thing and I wanted to overdub a train — you know those bells that clang when a steam engine pulls into a train station? So I wanted to do that. And I remember he said, “like will you stop? Will you just stop?” Now you should see what he hides in his records. Oh man, he’s just finishing his fifth album. He’s got stuff coming from fourteen directions. Sometimes I say to him, “why don’t you just make a nice record instead of doing all your secret little tricks?” You — and he laughs — weasel. And my oldest son Dave, he’s in charge of the digital world for the Warner Music Group through Rhino. So he’s in a world I don’t even know — I don’t even know what he does. But I know he does something. So and my middle son Mike, he would last three minutes in the record

business. The first guy that gave him any shit would be laying on the floor and looking up, because he has less of anything than any of us. So he’s in the furniture business, he manages a chain of furniture stores in the northeast, and loves music. He’s a country music junkie and a fifties junkie. And it’s an odd question to ask, but he always says you do what you do.

Well I think of it because my own kids, you know, they learned the word gig really soon. “Dad, do you have a gig tonight?” And I often sometimes would wonder what, if someone asked their friends what does your father do, “he plays gigs.” So I just was curious.

Yeah me and boys are cool. They’re my three best friends. We talk all the time, they all talk to each other, that part of my life really worked out nicely. And they look at me generally as a self-indulgent guy who’s managed to stay in the game.
